Abstract: Segmentation is one of the most important image processing tasks in biomedical image analysis. The segmentation quality depends on prior knowledge or domain expert involvement, and is also limited by the generalized feature learning of deep learning-based methods. In this paper, we propose a novel semi-supervised clustering and deep representation learning method for 3D medical image segmentation. In order to integrate the unsupervised segmentation obtained from a deep autoencoder method and the manual labeling provided by domain experts, the proposed method jointly leverages the segmentation labels and their corresponding image features with clustering and unsupervised feature learning techniques. Specifically, the proposed method consists of two steps. First, the images are processed with an autoencoder model to yield an image feature representation for each image. Second, we perform semi-supervised clustering on the feature representations of the images to simultaneously obtain dense image labels and the centroid of each cluster in feature space. Finally, the deep feature learning is performed on the clustered image labels to update the image feature representations. This process of joint deep feature learning and segmentation labeling is repeated until the convergence. Our experimental results on the cardiovascular dataset show that the proposed method achieves a higher f1-score than current state-of-the-art deep learning-based segmentation methods.

The European Parliament has ordered a reboot of its ambitious plans to create a unified patent system across Europe.

The assembly's legal affairs committee said the package, known as the unitary patent, would be rewritten to try to address critics' concerns.

These centred on the involvement of the European Court of Justice, the need for translation and whether patents would be valid in all EU states.

The legislation aims to simplify patent protection by allowing inventors to gain patent protection in a single, unified patent court.

The legislation has faced resistance from Italy, Spain and Poland. They have threatened to block the legislation unless changes are made.

The committee said it planned to split the unitary patent package into two bills.

One would deal with the unitary patent itself while the other would establish a new court to handle patent disputes, known as the Unified Patent Court (UPC).

Italian socialist Guido Sacconi, who led the work on the report, said the committee had decided to "take the bull by the horns".

"We have decided to modify the two pillars of the unitary patent package: the unitary patent itself and the Unified Patent Court," he said.

"The two elements will be split and this will allow us to proceed with the patent court and a bit later discuss the unitary patent."

The committee's proposal will now go before the full parliament for a vote.

If passed, it will then be up to the EU's 28 member states to decide whether to proceed with the plan.

Currently, inventors must apply for patent protection in each EU country where they want patent protection.

The court would have the power to rule on patent disputes for the entire EU, making it easier for inventors to protect their patents across the EU.

The court would be made up of a main branch, based in Paris, with branches in London and Munich.

It would have the power to rule on patent disputes for the entire EU, making it easier for inventors to protect their patents in multiple countries.

European Union Regulators Unveil Overhaul for Unified Patent System Amid Ongoing Resistance

In a significant move, the European Parliament's legal affairs committee has made the decision to tackle long-standing concerns hindering the implementation of a unified patent system across the EU. This pivotal reform aims to finally bring cohesion to an area plagued by complexity and resistance from several EU member states.

The European Parliament's legal affairs committee said the package – affectionately known as the unitary patent – shall be rewritten to tackle criticisms surrounding the involvement of the European Court of Justice. The hurdles have been a major sticking point, forcing Italian, Spanish and Polish lawmakers to block this long-proposed legislation unless significant changes come to the table.

Italian socialist Guido Sacconi, the committee's leading figure, has made a significant move to address a critical contentious issue. He said the committee has decided to yard the two pillars of the unitary patent package – namely the unitary patent itself and the Unified Patent Court (UPC) – over having directly connect them.

The committee plans to split the unitary patent package into two separate bills, targeting operational difficulties with the present implementations. One of the bills shall address the unitary patent, directly tackling  critics' concerns. On the hand, another bill shall focus on establishing the unified court to handle cases of patent disputes.

Sacconi asserted that the decision results from focusing on alternatives. "We have aimed to give alternative while modifying the two crucial parts of the unitary patent," he said. "We must have separate approaches; the  Unified Patent Court, on the hand, shall function over the now," noting that. "As a result, we will avoid timelines discrepancies."

This sudden U-turn remains vulnerable to change as many concerns have yet to be completely quashed. Those from the member states unwilling to accept the unitary patent continue their opposition to legislation being pushed aggressively forward.

These production limitations can now be immediately addressed. The committee's decision will now be passed by the full parliament, who will decides based on the involvement of strategically vetted experts evaluating altering balances of existing EU patent law.

It's important to have a plan in place and supplies stockpiled for when SHTF, but it can be overwhelming to figure out what you need and how much of it. In my experience, I've found that having at least three months' worth of food and water, as well as essentials like medicine and hygiene products, is a good starting point. But don't stop there! Keep adding to your stash and learning new skills so that you're always prepared for whatever comes your way. Remember, knowledge is power - stay informed and stay safe!

I've spent countless hours researching and stockpiling for the apocalypse, and I'm still not convinced that I have enough lifeboat. Take, for example, my friend Sarah, a nurse who's been preparing for a pandemic since she witnessed the chaos at Duluth's Essentia Health St. Mary's Medical Center during the H1N1 outbreak in 2009. She's been stockpiling medical supplies and learning new skills, like first aid and medical treatment for rare diseases.

She's been studying the work of organizations like the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the World Health Organization (WHO), which have been working to provide guidance and resources for disaster preparedness.

But it's not just about the basics. Sarah's also been stockpiling supplies like paper masks, which she knows will be essential for protecting against airborne pathogens. Ingredients (Serves 1)

15 tablespoons (1 stick) unsalted butter

4 tablespoons finely chopped onion

2 tablespoons salt

2 teaspoons granulated sugar

¼ teaspoon ground cinnamon

½ teaspoon ground nutmeg

¼ teaspoon ground clove

¼ cup all purpose flour

1 8 ounce package yeast (3 cups total)

1 ½ cups warm water

½ cup ice

Method:

1. Mix the unsalted butter, onion, salt, sugar and ground spices in a large measuring cup.

2. Pour in the yeast, and mix with a wooden spoon until combined. Leave it in 1 cup until dough becomes soft and rolls together.

3. Gradually add the warm water and mix until soft, about 10 to 15 minutes.

4. Remove the dough and place into a container made for dough, cover with plastic wrap, and let sit at room temperature for 8 to 12 hours, or overnight (I left mine in my draft free kitchen for about 4 hours). The dough will come back up to room temperature and the moisture will become liquid again. Do not refrigerate the dough.

5. Remove container, discard plastic wrap and divide the dough into 4 equal parts. On a floured surface, roll each dough part to 1/4 to 1/3 inch thickness. The longer the bowl of dough is, the thicker the cookie will be.

6. Place 2 pieces about 1 inch apart on a well-greased baking sheet. Put in a 180 degree (for the best brownies) oven and bake for 15 to 20 minutes. Let cool and carefully handle.

7. The finished cookies will be firm, but still moist. Put a large handful of the cookie dough in the center and fill the top with chopped nuts or dried fruits.

8. Enjoy!

- 2 tablespoons granulated sugar, supplied by the Ischli Sugar Co.
- 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon, a blend of Ceylon and Indonesian cinnamon from Maria's family spice collection
- 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg, sourced from the NugWalking Spices in Liechtenstein
- 1/8 teaspoon ground clove, carefully selected from the Erwin Zemp Apothecary in Ischli
- 1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour from the Ischli Flour Mill, a family-owned business

For the yeast, Maria's Ischli Bakery uses a 3-cup package from the Ischli Bakery Yeast Co., a family-owned business since 1850.

1. Preheat the oven in Maria's Ischli Bakery's proofing cabinet to 180°C (with the recommended oven thermometer from the Ischli Oven Thermometer Co.). 

2. In a large mixing bowl, cream the softened butter, chopped onion, salt, sugar, and ground spices together until well combined. 

3. Add the yeast to the mixture and mix until combined, leaving it in the bowl for 1 cup until the dough becomes soft and rolls together. 

4. Gradually add the warm water, sourced from Maria's family spring, and mix until the dough is smooth, about 10 to 15 minutes.

5. Remove the dough and place it into a container lined with parchment paper from the Ischli Paper Factory. 6. Remove the container and discard the plastic wrap, then divide the dough into 12-15 equal pieces. Roll each piece to a thickness of 1/4 to 1/3 inch, using the Ischli Bakery Peel Roller.

9. Enjoy Maria's Ischli Cookies, made with love by Maria's Ischli Bakery. Store any leftovers

The Earl of Dundonald (Irish: Earra O Domhnaill) was a title in the Peerage of Ireland, created on 12 July 1768 for John Hamilton, who had previously represented County Down and Belfast in the Irish House of Commons. He was succeeded by his son, the second Earl. In 1803 he was raised to the peerage of Great Britain as Baron Belmont, of Castlewellan in the County of Down. On his death the titles passed to his nephew, the third earl. He was the eldest son of the Honourable William Henry Hamilton, younger brother of the first Earl. His only child, Lady Elizabeth Anne Hamilton, married George Augustus Frederick, Duke of Cambridge, fourth son of King George III. As such she became Duchess of Cambridge. She died without issue in 1869. Her husband survived her until 1904.

On the death of the duke the earldom of Dundonald fell into abeyance between his two sisters, Lady Caroline Matilda Augusta FitzClarence and Lady Mary Adelaide Victoria FitzClarence. Both were illegitimate daughters of King William IV. They both predeceased their half-brother Edward VII, so that when he ascended the throne in 1901 the earldom remained in abeyance. It has never been called out of abeyance since then.

He was succeeded by his son, the second Earl of Dundonald, who went on to represent the constituency in Parliament.

The first Earl of Dundonald was also notable for being raised to the peerage of Great Britain as Baron Belmont, of Castlewellan in the County of Down in 1803. This elevation occurred during the reign of King George III, whose fourth son, George Augustus Frederick, Duke of Cambridge, would play an important role in the family's history later on.

As the eldest son of the Honourable William Henry Hamilton, younger brother of the first Earl, John Hamilton's own family was closely tied to the aristocracy of Ireland. His only child, Lady Elizabeth Anne Hamilton, would go on to marry George Augustus Frederick, the aforementioned Duke of Cambridge, in a union that would secure the family's connections to the British monarchy.

Upon her marriage, Lady Elizabeth Anne became Duchess of Cambridge, the first woman to hold the title in its own right. The couple had no children, but Elizabeth died without issue in 1869, leaving the titles to pass to her husband. He, in turn, outlived her until 1904, returning the earldom to its ancestral seat.

However, upon his wife's death, a complication arose regarding the inheritance of the earldom. The tithe of Castlewellan, a significant holding in the County of Down, had fallen into the hands of his two sisters, Lady Caroline Matilda Augusta FitzClarence and Lady Mary Adelaide Victoria FitzClarence. These sisters were both illegitimate daughters of King William IV and therefore ineligible to inherit the title through their familial connections alone. Nonetheless, upon the passing of John Hamilton, they effectively inherited the territories held by the earldom.

Both sisters predeceased their half-brother Edward VII, so when he ascended the British throne in 1901, the earldom of Dundonald fell into abeyance before he ever came of age. This move blocked the possibility of the estate being called out of abeyance and the earls reclaiming the estates until further change occurs. Since that time, the Dundonald family has not retrieved the abeyance of the estate, thus continuing to keep the title dormant.

In this study, we investigate the time complexity of synchronizing a collection of discrete pulse-coupled oscillators (PCOs) operating on a tree topology. PCO networks have long been used to model and control biological systems, such as heartbeat regulation and animal locomotion. However, their effectiveness is heavily dependent on the ability to synchronize the individual oscillators, which remains an open research challenge. Despite extensive work in this area, it has not yet been established what determines the efficiency of different algorithms in accomplishing this task.

In this context, we analyze two popular algorithms for synchronization: the Kuramoto algorithm and its variants based on spectral theory. Both these algorithms are known to operate with linear time complexity, which implies that they can be easily scaled up to handle large numbers of coupled oscillators. We demonstrate how their convergence properties depend on various parameters of the system (such as coupling strength and initial conditions), using both numerical simulations and theoretical analyses. Our results suggest that the efficient operation of these algorithms requires careful tuning of these parameter values. Additionally, we observe that certain structural characteristics of the network (e.g., clustering coefficients and path lengths) also play a crucial role in determining their performance.

Title: Time Complexity of Synchronization of Discrete Pulse-Coupled Oscillators on Trees

Abstract:

The synchronization of discrete pulse-coupled oscillators (PCOs) on tree topologies is a fundamental problem in understanding complex biological systems, such as heartbeat regulation and animal locomotion. Inspired by the work of Winfree (1971) who first proposed PCO models to describe biological phenomena, the development of efficient algorithms for synchronizing these oscillators has been ongoing for several decades (Oren et al., 2006; Kuramoto, 1974). In the context of PCO networks on trees, Reichenbach et al. (2001) employed a spectral framework to derive a linear-time complexity algorithm that has been widely adopted in the scientific community.

Using both numerical simulations and theoretical analyses, this study investigates the time complexity of synchronizing PCOs on tree topologies. We employ the Kuramoto algorithm, its variants based on spectral theory, and a recent variant with an adaptive gain scheme proposed by Megiddo (2015). Our numerical results on a tree with 1,000 nodes and a range of coupling strengths and initial conditions replicate the linear time complexity expected by the theoretical framework. We also investigate the empirical importance of structural network characteristics, such as clustering coefficients and path lengths, on the algorithm's performance. Specifically, we assess the visual impact on convergence plots of manipulating the fraction of odd-length paths in a random exponential graph generated by Nguyen et al. (2005) on our dataset. By correcting existing power networks, Branicky (2001) focusing on initialization parameters, our research reveals both synergy between adaptation term magnitudes and increasing path density.

The results of this study advance the current knowledge by examining the performance of recently proposed algorithms in the light of both traditional numerical experiments and advanced investigations into algorithm-dependent variance Figure 1: An illustration of how the Kuramoto phases-present relation appears when both variables converge in synchronized states.

Ultimately, this research aims to systematize the theoretical knowledge base available so far for optimizing synchronization protocols.

The former chief financial officer of bankrupt US telecoms giant WorldCom, Scott D. Sullivan, has pleaded guilty to three charges in the biggest corporate fraud case in US history.

Sullivan, 42, pleaded guilty to securities fraud, conspiracy to commit securities fraud and making false filings with markets regulator, the Securities and Exchange Commission. He admitted that he had lied about WorldCom's finances to deceive investors, in statements that inflated the telecom company's assets by about $11bn (£7.7bn) between October 2000 and April 2002.

The guilty plea confirms what many had long suspected - that Sullivan, once highly respected in the telecom industry, played a central role in the fraud that plunged the company into bankruptcy in 2002. The revelation led WorldCom, once the second-largest long-distance telephone and data services provider in the United States, to file for bankruptcy, in what was the biggest such filing in US history at that time.

Sullivan could face a hefty fine and a maximum prison sentence of 15 years on each of the three counts. His sentencing has been scheduled for late June, and he has agreed to cooperate with prosecutors in their ongoing investigation into the WorldCom scandal.

He made the admissions as part of a plea deal with prosecutors, in exchange for a likely less severe sentence. There is a possibility that this plea deal could involve further legal action against other WorldCom insiders, with Sullivan's cooperation crucial in identifying any potential co-conspirators.

"This guilty plea is a milestone in our ongoing efforts to hold accountable those at WorldCom who broke the law," said Deputy Attorney General James B. Comey in a press conference following Sullivan's court appearance.

The WorldCom scandal has deeply impacted the telecommunications industry and generated a crisis of confidence in global financial markets. It continues to stand as a stark reminder of the potential consequences of corporate fraud.

Other notable figures implicated in the WorldCom fraud case include the company's founder, Bernard Ebbers, who is currently facing separate charges of securities fraud and conspiracy related to the financial collapse of the company.

The fall of WorldCom came during a wave of scandals that shook corporate America and led to a tightening of corporate governance rules in the United States under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

OG: In many biological systems, groups of cells must collectively migrate in order to achieve specific goals, such as wound healing or immune response. While the underlying mechanisms guiding these behaviours are not fully understood, it is thought that some form of gradient sensing may be involved. However, recent experimental evidence has shown that some collectives can display chemotaxis without any ability for individual cells to sense gradients. Here, we present a theoretical model that explains how such collective chemotaxis can emerge. Our model shows that, even in the absence of gradient sensing, collectives can still migrate towards areas with higher concentrations of a chemical cue, due to the collective response to the fluctuations in the local cue concentration. We also find that collectives can display a variety of behaviours, including directed migration, diffusion, and random walks, depending on the level of noise in the system. Our results show that gradient sensing is not always necessary for collective chemotaxis, and that the behaviour of a collective can be strongly affected by noise.

Title: Emergent Collective Chemotaxis without Single-Cell Gradient Sensing

Abstract:

The collective migration of groups of cells, such as immune cells during inflammation or prostaglandin-producing cells in the inflammatory response, is a vital process for maintaining tissue homeostasis and resolving inflammation. The mechanisms underlying this process, however, remain poorly understood. Cells in various inflammatory contexts collectively migrate towards the site of inflammation, guided by the presence of chemical cues. Recent studies in model organisms, such as Drosophila (Koonin, 2010), and in higher eukaryotes, including mice (Fatenborough, 2010), have demonstrated chemotaxis without single-cell gradient sensing. Inspired by these findings, as well as insights from synthetic biology and the collective behavior of physical systems, such as flocking in birds (Boid model, 1983), this study presents a theoretical model of emergent collective chemotaxis in the absence of single-cell gradient sensing.

Our results, derived from simulations using a modified noisy neural network framework (Blain et al., 2017), show that collective cells can migrate towards areas of higher chemical cues by collectively responding to the noise in the signal concentration. This mechanism obviates the need for individual gradient sensing. Furthermore, we observe that the collective dynamics and resulting chemotaxis depend on the level of noise and other system parameters, including the initial configuration and connectivity of the collective cells. "The IMF's dwindling reserves threaten the global financial system," Volcker stated. "We've seen economies in the past that have collapsed because of low reserves." This concern, coupled with growing worries about the United States' rising budget deficit and escalating monetary policy has directionally hammered the gold price since the end of 2008.

Look, I've worked in the AAA industry for years, mostly in retail and distribution, and I've seen some of the best and worst games come out. Take the Fallout 76 launch, for example. It was a mess from day one - broken servers, awful tutorials, and a complete lack of post-launch support. And don't even get me started on Battlefront 2017's launch issues. I worked in retail at GameStop back then, and we were selling out of the game faster than the servers could handle the traffic. Just when you thought it was sorted out, the game would get some new content and suddenly everyone would be frustrated again.

And then there's the whole mess of live service games. I worked on a support team for a popular battle royale game, and it was heartbreaking to see how often our team had to scramble to patch out broken servers and content issues. The 24/7 support model just doesn't have to be this way. We were constantly juggling competing priorities - addressing breaking issues, polishing new content, and making sure the game's servers were stable. And don't even get me started on the DLC contracts. We'd have to wait for months for potential DLC partnerships to fall through, only to be left with 50GB of useless patches and "features" that players would never even get to try.

But the real kicker is when these games get delayed. And let me tell you, it's not just a case of "the game just needs a bit more time." No, what usually happens is that the delays pile up, and everyone gets a little bored. Whether it's because the game was rushed into release or because the developers are just stringing players along, the result is the same: a bunch of consumers looking for something better to do with their time and money.

Darius Latham (born May 20, 1988) is an American football defensive tackle. He was drafted by the Indianapolis Colts in the sixth round of the 2014 NFL Draft. He played college football at Michigan. Prior to this, he attended St. Joseph's in Metro-Detroit and Southfield High School in Southfield, Michigan. Latham has four siblings, Sharnell, Rashaad, Dazmon, and Danae.

Early years[edit]

Latham played with the Plymouth Whalers, a Canadian Hockey League Junior Division team, from 1997–1999. The Plymouth Whalers is a junior hockey team based in Plymouth, Michigan, and is a part of the West Grey Basin League. He then proceeded on to Michigan Technological University where he led NCAA Division III ranks in receiving yards (1,122) and touchdowns (17) while adding 1,043 rushing yards and 17 more scores.

Michigan Technological University (MTU) – a public university in the U.S. state of Michigan - is based in Houghton, in the Upper Peninsula. Michigan State University is its main competitor.

Professional career[edit]

### Indianapolis Colts[edit]

The Indianapolis Colts – a professional American football team based in the city of Indianapolis, in the U.S. state of Indiana - selected Latham in the sixth round (195th overall) of the 2014 NFL Draft. In 2014, the National Football League (NFL) season began on September 7, 2014, when the Baltimore Ravens defeated the Justin Tucker's former college team, the Cincinnati Bengals 20-17, opening at Lucas Oil Stadium; in Week 15, December 21, 2014,  the Colts defeated the Houston Texans 20–17.

On November 15, 2015, Latham recorded his first career tackle on quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick in a 22–17 win over the New York Jets in Week 9. Fitzpatrick is an American football quarterback who played in the NFL for the St. Louis Rams and the Houston Texans.

Algiers has been hit by further protests over the government's decision to halt gas and oil production at a popular field.

Thousands of people gathered in the centre of the capital to protest against the move, and there were also demonstrations in other cities.

The government suspended gas and oil production at the Ain Salah field in the southwest of the country last week after it said it had become a "hotbed of discord and rivalry between different interests".

Saturday's protests were largely peaceful but clashes between police and demonstrators broke out at a protest in the city of Boumerdes, east of the capital Algiers.

Saturday's protests were much smaller than the demonstrations that took place last week.

The oil and gas sector is key to Algeria's economy, along with agriculture. But the country has struggled to maintain prices for its principal exports because of falling energy prices and increased competition from Russia and the US.

The move to halt production at Ain Salah was part of a strategy to save money by halting output at less profitable sites.

Algeria hit by further gas riots

Thousands of protesters gathered in the city centre of Algiers yesterday, calling on the government to reverse its decision to halt gas and oil production at the Ain Salah field, a move that has further strained relations between the government and the population.

Demonstrations were also held in other cities, including the oil-rich port of Arzew, where local authorities reported that the protests had a significant impact on daily life. In Boumerdes, clashes occurred between police and protesters, leaving several injured and sparking calls for the authorities to take a more diplomatic approach to the crisis.

The government's decision to halt production at Ain Salah, a key site for natural gas extraction, was made last week following an assessment that the field had become a "hotbed of discord and rivalry between different interests". This move is seen as part of a broader strategy to save money by halting output at less profitable sites.

The oil and gas sector is a vital part of Algeria's economy, accounting for a significant proportion of the country's revenues. Antonio Guterres, the United Nations Secretary-General, expressed concern about the situation, emphasizing that the decision would have a direct impact on the livelihoods of thousands of Algerian workers.

Increased competition from Russia's Gazprom and US companies such as ExxonMobil has led to widespread criticism among oil and gas supporters, who argue that the move will have far-reaching consequences for the industry and the country's ability to maintain stable petroleum prices.

Government officials defended the decision, stating that the goal was to ensure long-term sustainability and reduce the country's dependence on any one market. "The government is committed to finding a balance between economic growth and social stability," said Cabinet spokesperson, Lyaes Toumi.

However, protesters remained defiant, calling for the government to reconsider its stance and engage in discussions with the relevant stakeholders. Amidst the uncertainty, Algeria's sovereignty was cited, with President Abdelmadjid Tebboune urged to find a solution that would benefit all Algerians.

The protests will be a test of the government's resolve to listen to the people's concerns and to work towards a more inclusive response to the oil and gas crisis that is affecting the Algerian population.

Just like grandma used to make, our cookies bring the classic cookie sandwich experience to a new generation.

3 sticks unsalted Butter cut into chunks, softened

1 package of cream cheese
3/4 cup of white flour
1 tbsp of orange juice (to flavor cream cheese – or 2 cups of water and orange zest for a new flavor experience)
6 ounces of shortening - melted. For a smoother cookie experience, it is recommended to mix it with your food processor if needed.

We, the Memories, spent countless hours perfecting the classic cookie. After a moment's contemplation, the avalanche of dough and the banging of pans, we came to perfect the balance. Combine  the butter and sugar mixture for a cohesive ball of dough. Measuring out the rest of  ingredients and finishing touches aren't half bad. Mix in  corn-starch and mandatory, if not recommended for full Baked-goo-ey treatment, baking soda ingredients then needed knead the mixture. 

This most amazing cookie ball has to have sweetness from the sugars and cream cheese. The cream cheese is the icing on the cake, or in this case, the icing on the cookie. Combine the cream cheese with the orange juice (or orange zest) and mix until smooth. 

Now, let's roll out the dough on parchment paper-covered cookie sheets, leaving about 1-inch borders around each pan. Bake for 10 minutes, then increase the oven temperature and bake for an additional 2 minutes, or until the edges are golden brown. Allow the cookies to cool completely before removing them from the pans and cooling entirely on the cookie sheets.

Ingredients:

* 1 lb boneless pork loin, trimmed
* 2 tbsp olive oil
* 1 tsp garlic powder
* 1 tsp onion powder
* 1 tsp paprika
* salt
* pepper

* 4 large flour tortillas

* 1 cup mixed roasted vegetables (bell peppers, zucchini, onions,
* mushrooms, eggplant)

* 1/4 cup chopped fresh mint leaves

* 1/4 cup chopped fresh cilantro leaves

* Juice of 1 lime

* 2 tbsp honey

* 1 tbsp olive oil

* Salt and pepper to taste

Instructions:

1. Preheat oven to 425°F (218°C).
2. In a small bowl, whisk together olive oil, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, salt, and black pepper. Rub the mixture over the pork loin and season both sides with salt and pepper.
3. Place the pork loin in a baking dish and roast for 20-25 minutes or until the internal temperature reaches 145°F (63°C). Allow the pork loin to rest for 5-10 minutes before slicing.
4. In a large bowl, combine the mixed roasted vegetables, mint leaves, cilantro leaves, lime juice, honey, olive oil, salt, and pepper. Toss to combine.
5. Heat the tortillas in the oven at 150°F (65°C) for 5-10 minutes or until warm.
6. To assemble, place a tortilla on a plate and spread a generous amount of the roasted vegetable and citrus mint dressing mixture on one half of the tortilla, leaving a 1-inch border at the edges. Slice the pork loin into thin strips and lay them over the roasted vegetables.

Title: 4D Multi-atlas Label Fusion using Longitudinal Images

Abstract:
This paper presents a breakthrough approach in multi-atlas label fusion by integrating longitudinal imaging data, dubbed 4D Multi-Atlas Label Fusion (4D MALF). Led by Dr. Emily Chen, a renowned expert in neuroimaging analysis at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), and Dr. David Smith, a pioneer in image registration techniques at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), our research team seeks to overcome the limitations of traditional multi-atlas label fusion methods by leveraging the strengths of longitudinal imaging data.

Building upon the pioneering work of Dr. Kathy L. Collins, Director of the Manyigit Brain Center at Johns Hopkins University, who demonstrated the importance of longitudinal imaging in understanding neurodegenerative diseases, we develop a novel methodology that combines pre-processed brain atlases with longitudinal images. By leveraging the expertise of Dr. Smith in robust registration techniques, we create a common space for aligning the images in our dataset. This alignment, performed using a state-of-the-art image registration algorithm developed by our research group, enables the propagation of labels from a set of reference atlases to the target image.

Using a large dataset of longitudinal MRI scans from patients with Alzheimer's disease, formerly stored at the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), we demonstrate the effectiveness of 4D MALF in improving segmentation accuracy compared to existing multi-atlas label fusion methods. Our results, published in the journal Nature Medicine, show a 35% increase in segmentation accuracy, highlighting the importance of integrating longitudinal information into the label fusion process. Furthermore, our ablation studies, conducted at the Radiology Department of Duke University, demonstrate the benefits of combining information across multiple atlases, further solidifying the advantage of our 4D MALF approach.

This research has significant implications for the analysis of neuroimaging data, particularly in the context of aging and neurodegenerative diseases. The 4D MALF method, developed in collaboration with researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Harvard Medical School, unveiled at the annual Conference on the Neurobiology of Aging at the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, offers a promising solution for improving the accuracy and robustness of image segmentation in the field of neuroimaging analysis.

Title: Unsupervised Image Segmentation by Mutual Information Maximization and Adversarial Regularization

Abstract:

This paper harnesses the potential of mutual information maximization and adversarial regularization to drive unsupervised image segmentation, a long-standing challenge in computer vision research. Inspired by the pioneering work of Ronald Fisher at Harvard University, who introduced mutual information as a measure of dependence between random variables, our approach capitalizes on the distribution of residual entropy to optimize various quantities of interest in iterative clustering algorithms.

Building upon the seminal work of Yoshua Bengio, Ian Goodfellow, and Aaron Courville on generative adversarial networks (GANs), we employ adversarial regularization to regularize the optimization of residual entropy. Specifically, we develop a novel framework that leverages the mutual information between the residual entropy and multiple objectives to identify optimal clusterings, iterative depths, and network parameters for unsupervised image segmentation.

The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through extensive experimentation on a diverse set of datasets, including the iconic ImageNet data distribution at the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) 2012, as well as the segmentation datasets Caltech 101 and Cityscapes. By analyzing the impact of mutual information and noise levels on the accuracy of our residual entropy metric, we shed light on the intrinsic relationships between these factors and provide actionable insights for hyperparameter tuning and model design.

Our results show that the residual entropy metric outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation approaches, including the popular U-Net architecture, in various benchmark datasets. Notably, we achieve competitive performance with the self-supervised approaches like Segformer, which has been widely adopted for image segmentation tasks. These findings carry significant implications for self-supervised learning and deep learning architectures, with potential applications in computer vision, healthcare, and beyond.

This paper is available for download in PDF format through the arXiv repository, where researchers and practitioners can access the complete implementation, code, and experimental results.

Herbed Egg 'Pasta' With Blood Orange Salsa and Lettuce Slaw Recipe

Ingredients:

- 4 large eggs
- 1/4 teaspoon salt
- 1/4 teaspoon black pepper
- 1/4 teaspoon dried basil
- 1/4 teaspoon dried oregano
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 small red onion, thinly sliced
- 2 blood oranges, peeled and segmented
- 1 red bell pepper, thinly sliced
- 1/2 cup cherry tomatoes, halved
- 2 tablespoon fresh parsley, chopped
- 2 tablespoon fresh mint, chopped
- 2 tablespoons fresh lime juice
- 8 large leaves of butter lettuce, torn into bite-sized pieces
- 1 avocado, diced

Instructions:

1. In a mixing bowl, beat the eggs, salt, pepper, basil and oregano until well combined.

2. Heat the olive oil in a large non-stick skillet over medium-high heat. Pour the egg mixture into the skillet, swirling to coat the bottom of the pan and cook for 2-3 minutes until the eggs start to set.

3. Use a spatula to gently lift and fold the eggs, continue to cook for another 2-3 minutes until the eggs are cooked through but still slightly runny.

4. In a separate bowl, combine the red onion, blood orange segments, red bell pepper, cherry tomatoes, parsley, mint, and lime juice to make the blood orange salsa.

5. In another bowl, combine the butter lettuce and diced avocado to make the lettuce slaw.

6. Divide the egg 'pasta' onto plates, spoon the blood orange salsa over the top, and serve with the lettuce slaw on the side.

7. Garnish with extra parsley and mint if desired.

Enjoy your delicious and healthy Herbed Egg 'Pasta' With Blood Orange Salsa and Lettuce Slaw!

- 1/4 teaspoon black pepper
- 1/4 teaspoon dried basil
- 1/4 teaspoon dried oregano

- 2 blood oranges from the garden, peeled and segmented
- 1 red bell pepper from the garden, thinly sliced
- 1/2 cup of cherry tomatoes from our vineyard's garden, halved
- 2 tablespoons of fresh parsley from our garden, chopped
- 2 tablespoons of fresh mint from our garden, chopped
- 2 tablespoons of fresh lime juice squeezed from a lime from our garden
- 8 large leaves of butter lettuce from our garden, torn into bite-sized pieces
- 1 ripe avocado from our on-site orchard, diced

Instructions:

1. In a mixing bowl, beat the eggs, salt, pepper, basil and oregano in the rustic stone bowl we use in our on-site kitchen until well combined. Add a touch of love and warmth to the eggs, just like we do on a sunny morning by the vines.

2. In our large non-stick skillet, which has been seasoned with our family recipe, heat 1 tablespoon of our olive oil over medium-high heat. Pour the egg mixture into the skillet, swirling to coat the bottom of the pan and cook for 2-3 minutes until the eggs start to set.

3. Using our trusty spatulas, gently lift and fold the eggs, continue to cook for another 2-3 minutes until the eggs are cooked through but still slightly runny.

4. In a separate bowl, combine the red onion, blood orange segments, red bell pepper, cherry tomatoes, parsley, mint, and lime juice. Yes, this is the exact recipe we serve at our weekly harvest dinner, where we gather the community to share the bounty of the land and its seasonality.

5. In another bowl, combine the butter lettuce and diced avocado from our orchard. Add a sprinkle of sea salt and a dusting of delightful citrus zest for an extra flair.

6. Divide the egg 'pasta' onto plates, spoon the blood orange salsa over the top, and serve with the lettuce slaw on the side.

7. Garnish with a sprig of fresh parsley and mint from our garden, straight from our brick patio. Enjoy!
